page: Microsoft Azure M32bds_v3 is a memory-optimized virtual machine belonging to the MBDSMediumMemoryv3 family, running on the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor. It features a dedicated Intel Xeon 8473C x86_64 processor with 32 vCPUs, consisting of 16 physical cores with 2 threads per core, operating at a clock speed of 4.0 GHz. The processor is equipped with a 105 MB L3 cache and supports advanced instruction sets, including Intel Advanced Vector Extensions (AVX-512) and Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX) for accelerated matrix operations. The instance is configured with 256.0 GB of RAM, providing a high memory-to-vCPU ratio of 8.0 GB per core, and includes 410 GB of local storage.

In benchmark evaluations, the M32bds_v3 demonstrates strong performance in memory-intensive and specific computational tasks. It achieved a Geekbench single-core score of 2197.0 and a multi-core score of 18223.0, both falling into the strong tier. Single-threaded gzip compression reached 32.77 GB/sec, and multi-threaded bzip3 decompression scored 213.19 GB/sec, indicating robust data processing capabilities. Memory bandwidth tests showed a cached read speed of 2766.64 GB/sec and an uncached large-block read speed of 181.54 GB/sec. For database operations, the instance processed 44.19 million Redis SET operations per second, while static web serving throughput reached 52.78 GB/sec.

While the server excels in memory capacity and standard computational tasks, it exhibits performance tradeoffs in large-scale machine learning workloads due to the absence of dedicated GPU hardware. LLM inference benchmarks for a 70B parameter model dropped to a weak 2.74 tokens/sec for text generation, though smaller 135M model text generation performed strongly at 312.22 tokens/sec. Given its high memory density, dedicated CPU allocation, and local storage, the M32bds_v3 is highly cost-efficient for memory-bound enterprise workloads. It is best suited for relational databases, in-memory caching layers like Redis, data compilation, and medium-scale web serving.
